$schema_description: Course Study App — Production Lecture Lab Additions Template. Maps lecture slides to hands-on laboratory exercises, terminal commands, tool invocations, and practical debugging pitfalls across any course. Slide titles, sections, and deck metadata are defined centrally in slides_index.json and inherited automatically — do NOT repeat them here. All textual fields support full Markdown and LaTeX math ($inline$ or $$display$$ with double-escaped '\\'). The first slide entry below provides field-by-field instructions; subsequent entries show real examples.

_file_naming_and_placement.rule: Use a consistent lecture prefix matching the literature and exam addition files for this lecture (e.g., 'L1_literature.json', 'L1_exams.json', and 'L1_labs.json' all sit inside 'Code/src/data/lecture_additions/').

markdown_and_latex_support.note: ALL TEXTUAL FIELDS SUPPORT FULL GITHUB-FLAVORED MARKDOWN AND KATEX MATH ($inline$ or $$display$$).
markdown_and_latex_support.mandatory_json_backslash_rule: CRITICAL: In JSON strings, the backslash '\' is the JSON escape character. Every LaTeX command MUST use double backslashes '\\'. For example, write '$\alpha$', '$\text{ms}$', '$$\frac{a}{b}$$', and '$O(M \times N)$'. Never write unescaped '\t' or '\f'. Escape literal dollar signs in prose as \$.
markdown_and_latex_support.code_and_math_rules: Use backticks (`$var`) exclusively for code, shell syntax, packet headers, and script variables; use dollar signs ($math$) exclusively for LaTeX math (never nest backticks in math). Never output raw HTML/MathML tags like <span class='katex'> or <math>. Escape literal dollar signs in prose as \$.

lecture_id: INSTRUCTION: Unique identifier string matching an 'id' from slides_index.json (e.g. 'lectures-module-1', 'l1-crypto-intro'). Deck title, document filename, and slide titles are resolved automatically from slides_index.json.

slides._comment: SCHEMA & FIELD INSTRUCTIONS: Slide lab addition schema definition. Slide title and section are inherited automatically from slides_index.json.
slides.slide: INSTRUCTION: Integer (1-indexed physical sheet/slide number from slides_index.json) where these additions belong. Must be an integer >= 1.

lab_additions.lab_id: INSTRUCTION: Unique identifier matching an 'id' in labs_index.json (e.g., 'lab-1-crypto', 'lab-2-netsec').
lab_additions.task_id: INSTRUCTION: Unique identifier matching a 'task_id' in labs_index.json (e.g., 'task-1-2', 'task-2-1'). Allows multiple distinct tasks sharing the same page to be cited and differentiated precisely.
lab_additions.lab_title: MARKDOWN FIELD: Canonical title of the lab assignment (e.g., 'Lab 1: Cryptographic Primitives & PKI').
lab_additions.task_number: INSTRUCTION: Human-readable task, step, or exercise identifier (e.g., 'Task 1.2', 'Exercise 3', 'Part B').
lab_additions.relevance_summary: MARKDOWN FIELD: Concise 1-2 sentence explanation of how the theoretical concept on this slide directly applies to the lab exercise.
lab_additions.practical_guidance: MARKDOWN FIELD: Detailed engineering walkthrough explaining what students perform in this lab: tools invoked, options configured, expected observations, and validation steps. Supports full Markdown (**bold**, `code`, bullet points) and LaTeX math ($...$).
code_or_commands: INSTRUCTION: Array of exact shell commands, terminal invocations, script snippets, or tool configurations (e.g. 'openssl enc -aes-128-ecb ...', 'tcpdump -i eth0 -w trace.pcap').
lab_additions.common_pitfalls: MARKDOWN FIELD: Common student mistakes, subtle bugs, missing parameters, byte alignment gotchas, or environment errors to watch out for.

citations.id: INSTRUCTION: Identifier matching an 'id' in labs_index.json (e.g., 'lab-1-crypto').
citations.task_id: INSTRUCTION: Identifier matching a 'task_id' in labs_index.json (e.g., 'task-1-2'). The app automatically maps this task to its exact page in the lab manual PDF without needing a hardcoded page number.

slides._comment: EXAMPLE 1: CONCRETE SLIDE WITH CRYPTOGRAPHIC OPENSSL LAB ADDITION

lab_additions.relevance_summary: Direct practical demonstration of ECB mode pattern leakage on structured data compared to CBC/CTR mode IV randomization.
lab_additions.practical_guidance: In this exercise, you encrypt a 24-bit uncompressed bitmap image (`tux.bmp`) using AES in ECB mode versus CBC mode. Because ECB encrypts identical 128-bit plaintext blocks into identical ciphertext blocks, pixel patterns from the original image remain plainly visible in the encrypted output.
lab_additions.common_pitfalls: Encrypting the entire BMP file including its 54-byte header corrupts the image magic bytes (`BM`), causing image viewers to reject the file. You must preserve the unencrypted 54-byte BMP header to view the visual pattern leakage.

slides._comment: EXAMPLE 2: CONCRETE SLIDE WITH PACKET CAPTURE / WIRESHARK LAB ADDITION

lab_additions.lab_title: Lab 2: Network Traffic Analysis & Intrusion Detection
lab_additions.relevance_summary: Inspecting live Wireshark traces to identify the 1-RTT TLS 1.3 handshake sequence, `ClientHello` KeyShare extension, and server certificate encryption.
lab_additions.practical_guidance: Students capture an HTTPS connection to a test server using `tshark` or `tcpdump`, export the session pre-master secrets via the `SSLKEYLOGFILE` environment variable, and observe how Wireshark transitions from plaintext `ClientHello`/`ServerHello` to encrypted records.
lab_additions.common_pitfalls: Confusing TLS 1.2 (where Server Certificate is transmitted in the clear) with TLS 1.3 (where Certificate and CertificateVerify are encrypted under the Server Handshake Traffic Secret).
